motion: Mass collection of U.S. phone records violates the Fourth Amendment

dropped_turns.speaker: PRO
dropped_turns.text: If officials may collect every person's calling history without suspicion, what meaningful limit stops them from assembling a permanent map of every private association they make?

dropped_turns.speaker: CON
dropped_turns.text: After a threat, investigators compare a known number with routing records and find its network. That lead can prevent harm without reading speech, proving collection need not violate the amendment.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Welcome. Tonight's motion is: mass collection of U.S. phone records violates the Fourth Amendment. Karen argues for it, and Amy argues against it. Each has thirty seconds to open, followed by two and a half minutes of crossfire, then thirty-second closings; I will give a ten-second cue. Please address each other directly and stay with the motion.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: Mass collection turns private patterns into a permanent map of ordinary life. The Fourth Amendment protects people from broad government searches, not merely from officers touching a phone. When officials gather everyone's calling history before suspicion, they search first and justify later. That reverses the constitutional safeguard. That's all, thank you.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: All right, let's give Amy a chance to reply.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Phone records are routing facts held by service companies, not the content of anyone's conversation. The government may examine those records under lawful process.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: But that label misses the harm: a list-

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: No. Let Amy come in. Please.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: rather than private papers. That limited review is not a search of a person's private life at all under the amendment as written today.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Well, now ten.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: The amendment restrains unreasonable searches, and obtaining company-held routing data reasonably does not violate it. That's all, thank you.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Now we move on to round two. And round two is where the debaters address each other in turn. You get two and a half minutes from the moment I finish speaking. I will give you a ten-second warning.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Karen says collection reverses safeguards, but records already exist for billing and connection. Receiving them does not enter a home, read speech, or seize a device.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: The real protection is building strict limits on who may use records, how long agencies retain them, and whether workers face discipline for misuse. Strong oversight prevents abuse.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Can we please go back to the question at hand? We're going to go back to the question at issue.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: The question is whether mass collection itself violates the Fourth Amendment, and it does because it gathers intimate associations without individualized cause. Oversight cannot erase an unconstitutional search.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Public trust also suffers when secret programs operate without clear notice, though public confidence alone is not the legal test. The legal question remains search, and collection is not one.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: Amy's point that collection is not a search ignores what the government learns by combining records: relationships, routines, and vulnerable moments. That is exactly the privacy the amendment shields.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: No collection of phone records violates the Fourth Amendment. A record of numbers and times is a company document, so receiving it does not invade a person's protected space.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: Amy's absolute claim fails because mass collection is not simply receiving one company's document. It creates a detailed portrait of every person's associations, which is the invasion.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: This collection of phone records violates the Fourth Amendment. When officials sweep up everyone's patterns, the program becomes too broad, yet the amendment still does not forbid all routine records.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: So it's not much of no collection of phone records violates the Fourth Amendment if this collection of phone records violates the Fourth Amendment, is it?

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: My first statement addresses ordinary acquisition, while my second addresses this vast program's practical reach. A rule can recognize records as nonprivate yet condemn an agency's careless handling of them.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: No, those statements cannot both define the law, because her first leaves no room for this program. Amy now admits scale changes the privacy invasion, which shows mass collection is-

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Scale does not transform a business record into private content, and that is the mistake. A warehouse may hold many ordinary files without each file becoming a constitutional search.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: I agree content deserves especially strong protection, but metadata can reveal nearly as much through patterns. The government's decision to gather it indiscriminately violates the Fourth Amendment.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Ten seconds, ten seconds.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Karen's pattern claim assumes inference equals a search, but an inference is not entry into private life. The amendment regulates government searches-

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: That's time. Now we move on to round three. Karen will go first, arguing for the resolution. Karen, the floor is yours.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: Phone records are not empty labels. In bulk, they reveal who we rely on, where our lives turn, and what associations we keep. The amendment requires a reason before government builds that map, not a promise to use it carefully afterward. Mass collection therefore violates the Fourth Amendment. That's all, thank you.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Amy, you have the last word.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Karen treats useful patterns as if they were private papers, but the amendment's line is government intrusion into protected life. Phone companies create routing records to connect calls, and lawful access to those records does not inspect conversation or enter a home. The real danger is giving constitutional labels to every administrative record, because that would.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: I'll give you ten more seconds to nail this.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: freeze ordinary investigations, even when officials seek only routing facts, not anyone's words or private space. That's all, thank you.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Thank you both for a thoughtful debate. This concludes our discussion of mass collection and the Fourth Amendment.
